evidence: Tell students that they will now review their Sky notebooks and pick two entries to share with the visitors.
rationale: Students share relevant and accurate information about the sun, moon, and stars through multiple modes. In Work Time A, students select two Sky notebook entries with accurate information to share with visitors. In Work Time B, students practice answering questions about patterns in the sky using the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol. In Work Time C, students practice reading their 'What the Sun Sees' poems aloud. The lesson explicitly directs students to share through notebooks (visual/print), oral responses to questions (dialogue), and oral reading of poems, satisfying the variety-of-modes requirement.

evidence: 'What part of your poem are you most proud and most excited to share with a visitor?' (Responses will vary.)
rationale: The lesson includes a moment where students discuss a personal preference about their own writing: "What part of your poem are you most proud and most excited to share with a visitor?" This touches on a personal writing preference, partially meeting the first clause. However, the discussion is narrowly about pride in a specific product (the poem), not about broader reading and writing preferences. The second clause — referring to specific techniques, topics, modes, or genres that resonate most — is not met: no activity asks students to name or reflect on preferred techniques, topics, modes, or genres. The lesson is focused on presentation preparation, not on articulating reading/writing preferences.

evidence: Using a total participation technique, invite responses from the group: 'What should you keep in mind while you are selecting entries from your Sky notebook to share? What criteria should those entries meet?' (neat writing, accurate information, entries that show different information and times of day)
rationale: In Work Time A, students develop and apply knowledge of audience (visitors) and purpose (to teach about the sun, moon, and stars) to select Sky notebook entries to share. Students respond to the question about what criteria entries should meet (neat writing, accurate information, entries showing different information and times of day), demonstrating their understanding of purpose. Students then review their own notebooks and select two entries, evaluating which entries best achieve the purpose of teaching visitors based on quality and content criteria. All three clauses are met through this selection and evaluation process.

evidence: Guide students through four rounds of the protocol using the following questions: 'What is a pattern that the sun, moon, or stars follow? How would you describe that pattern?' 'What is something you learned about the sun, moon, or stars that you did not know before?' 'What do you still wonder about the sun, moon, or stars?'
rationale: The "discuss topics" clause is met: during Work Time B, students use the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol to discuss sun, moon, and stars topics with a partner ("Guide students through four rounds of the protocol using the following questions: 'What is a pattern that the sun, moon, or stars follow?'…"). Students also share out with the whole group afterward. However, the remaining clauses are not met. Students do not collaboratively investigate questions — the protocol has them answer pre-set teacher questions, not pursue inquiry together. There is no collaborative problem-solving activity. Students do not collaboratively explore or create texts — they individually select notebook entries and individually practice reading their already-completed poems aloud to a partner (sharing, not co-creating). The lesson is preparation for a celebration, not collaborative text creation or investigation.

evidence: 'What is something you learned about the sun, moon, or stars that you did not know before?' … Invite a few students to share out what they discussed with their partners during the protocol.
rationale: The standard's four purposes (build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, share information and ideas) form an OR list; any one student-performed purpose satisfies the clause. Students make use of their module texts (Sky notebooks, "What the Sun Sees" poems) to share information and ideas about the sun, moon, and stars with partners. In Work Time B, students discuss questions such as "What is something you learned about the sun, moon, or stars that you did not know before?" and "What is a pattern that the sun, moon, or stars follow? How would you describe that pattern?" — actively using texts to build and share knowledge. In Work Time C, students read their poems aloud to a partner via the Pinky Partners protocol, again sharing information drawn from texts. The student is the actor throughout: selecting notebook entries, discussing content with partners, and presenting poems aloud.
standard_raw_text: Make use of texts to build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, and share information and ideas. (I/C)
